title: Keith Moon - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 168,274. Keith John Moon, born 23 August 1946, Central Middlesex Hospital, Wembley; died 7 September 1978, Mayfair, of a clomethiazole overdose, aged 32. Alperton Secondary Modern; the Sea Cadet Corps band at twelve, bugle then drums; lessons from Carlo Little of Screaming Lord Sutch's band at ten shillings each. Influences: jazz, American surf music and R&B (Hal Blaine as an example), Gene Krupa his favourite ('whose flamboyant style he later copied'), DJ Fontana, Tony Meehan, Viv Prince; Motown; the Beach Boys. Auditioned April 1964 at 17 in place of Doug Sandom (broke a bass drum pedal and two heads); told Ringo Starr he had 'just been filling in for the last fifteen years'. Style 'emphasised tom-toms, cymbal crashes, and drum fills'; Daltrey: he 'just instinctively put drum fills in places that other people would never have thought of putting them'; Entwistle: he played faster or slower by mood, 'He'd play zig-zag. That's why he had two sets of tom-toms. He'd move his arms forward like a skier'; Jon Astley: 'You didn't think he was keeping time, but he was.' Tony Fletcher: Who's Next his best drumming. Disliked drum solos ('Drum solos are boring!', Madison Square Garden, 1974). With Ginger Baker a pioneer of two bass drums in rock. Kit: Ludwig and Zildjian 1964-65; Premier from late 1965, a red sparkle kit with two high toms first; a larger kit without a hi-hat in 1966, the hat later reinstated; the 'Pictures of Lily' kit (1967-69): two 22-inch bass drums, two 16-inch floor toms, three mounted toms (reissued 2006 as 'Spirit of Lily'); timbales, gongs and timpani from 1970. Melody Maker, 1970: 'I suppose as a drummer, I'm adequate. I've got no real aspirations to be a great drummer.' Rankings: no. 1 in The New Book of Rock Lists; Rolling Stone readers no. 2 (2011), Rolling Stone no. 2 (2016); Modern Drummer Hall of Fame 1982; Rock and Roll Hall of Fame 1990 with the Who. Ray Davies: 'Keith Moon changed the sound of drumming.' Neil Peart and Clem Burke cite him. Kenney Jones replaced him (November 1978); Simon Phillips toured in 1989; Zak Starkey, his godson ('Uncle Keith', who gave him a drum kit), the Who's drummer 1996-2025. Close friendship with Ringo Starr.

title: How to play drums like Keith Moon (Tyler Golsen, Far Out, 23 August 2022)
notes: His set-up 'relied heavily on rack toms and crash cymbals'; 'Moon completely excised the hi-hat from his setup' (an overstatement of the 1966-69 kits: the tabs read have hats on most songs); two bass drums, most audible on Live at Leeds. My Generation: 'the kind of wrist dexterity largely reserved for jazz drummers'; he could 'stop and start along with the pauses for Daltrey's lead vocals'. Advice: 'fills that follow vocal patterns'. Restraint in Bargain, Underture, Love Reign O'er Me. Entwistle: 'he always played with the vocals'. Daltrey: 'Pete and John as two knitting needles and Keith was the ball of wool.' Townshend: his drumming 'an expression of his personality and his ego and his grandiosity'.

title: Keith Moon Elected to Hall of Fame in 1982 (T. Bruce Wittet, Modern Drummer, from the September 2003 issue)
notes: Moon, interviewed October 1978: 'You can't work out things too much'; 'Sometimes I'll build up with timpani; sometimes I'll build up on a cymbal or with a roll around the kit.' 'There are so many variations on each effect.' Mike Portnoy: 'controlled chaos': 'the constant pulsating 8th notes on the kick drums', 'the furious stampede of constant tom fills', 'the steady whirlwind of crash cymbals'.

title: Who's Next - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 119,588. Track (UK, 27 August 1971) and Decca (US, 2 August 1971); produced by the Who, Glyn Johns associate producer; recorded April-June 1971, mostly at Olympic, Barnes; the backing track of Won't Get Fooled Again at Stargroves with the Rolling Stones Mobile. Baba O'Riley's organ from Townshend's demo ('two or three thousand edits'); Won't Get Fooled Again's Lowrey organ through an EMS VCS3; played live to a backing tape. Moon's drumming 'has a distinctly different style from earlier albums, being more formal and less reliant on long drum fills'.

title: I Can't Explain - Wikipedia
notes: Decca (US, 19 December 1964) and Brunswick (UK, 15 January 1965); produced by Shel Talmy; recorded early November 1964 at Pye (citation needed). Keith Moon: drums, backing vocals.

title: My Generation (album) - Wikipedia
notes: Brunswick, 3 December 1965 (US as The Who Sings My Generation, Decca, 25 April 1966); produced by Shel Talmy at IBC, 12 April to 12 November 1965. Moon: drums. The US edit of The Kids Are Alright cut a break 'laden with manic drum rolls and guitar feedback'; Unterberger: 'the most ferociously powerful guitars and drums yet captured on a rock record'.

title: Tommy (The Who album) - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 153,076. Decca (US, 19 May 1969), Track (UK, 23 May 1969); produced by Kit Lambert at IBC and Morgan, 19 September 1968 to 7 March 1969. Moon played a double bass drum kit owned by roadie Tony Haslam after Premier stopped lending him gear; his idea was Tommy's Holiday Camp. Pinball Wizard single, 7 March 1969.

title: Quadrophenia - Wikipedia
notes: Read to character 100,000 of 132,822. Track/MCA, 26 October 1973 (UK 29 October); produced by the Who, largely by Townshend; Olympic, Ramport and Ronnie Lane's mobile, May-June 1972 and May-September 1973. After Who's Next Moon 'returned to his established drumming style'; sang Bell Boy. 5:15 single 5 October 1973, after Top of the Pops on 4 October.

title: Who Are You - Wikipedia
notes: Polydor (UK, 18 August 1978), MCA (US, 21 August 1978); produced by Glyn Johns and Jon Astley; Ramport, Olympic, RAK and others, September 1977 to April 1978. His drumming had 'noticeably deteriorated'; he could not play the 6/8 of Music Must Change, whose drums were removed; Entwistle: 'really out of condition'; Townshend: 'getting so uneven that recording was almost impossible'. Apart from the title track, all the drums were recorded in the last two weeks at Ramport.

title: Rolling Stone Readers Pick Best Drummers of All Time (2011)
notes: Readers' poll: Moon second, after John Bonham. Not read in full; the placing as Wikipedia reports it.

title: The Who, Won't Get Fooled Again, Shepperton Studios, 25 May 1978 (filmed for The Kids Are Alright)
notes: Watched (frames every three to five seconds, 0:20-3:20) for the likeness and the kit: Moon in a loose cream peasant shirt with dark embroidered swirls and a laced neck, headphones held on with tape, short dark hair, clean-shaven; a chrome kit with a row of rack toms, a big gong behind him.
